summary:
Kelantan stands under the national framework of Malaysia. Sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" for any person regardless of gender or consent, carrying a maximum of 20 years plus whipping; these provisions are not limited to Malaysians and apply to visitors. Sodomy was first criminalised in 1871.

Kelantan maintains Sharia enactments that criminalise cross-dressing or "a man posing as a woman", with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. These state offences reach Muslims only. Enforcement is carried out by the state Islamic religious department, and the law contains no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing.

The Federal Court struck down 16 provisions of the Kelantan Syariah Criminal Code Enactment 2019 in February 2024 on federalism grounds, leaving the federal Penal Code offences fully intact. The Kelantan state legislature responded by passing the Syariah Criminal Offences (Kelantan) Bill 2026 on 13 August 2026, which replaces those 16 struck provisions and legislates covering aurat, gender change, and safeguarding the modesty of private parts. Clause 15 requires Muslims to safeguard the sanctity and modesty of their private parts in accordance with Islamic law, and the state's legislative direction explicitly regulates gender-change matters under Islamic criminal law, with enforcement beginning in 2026.

The new provisions are in force and are being applied by the Kelantan Syariah courts. A case in February 2026, which preceded the bill, was the first Kelantan Syariah Court case involving gender change.

For a non-Muslim foreign visitor, the Sharia cross-dressing and gender-change offences do not apply, but the Penal Code does. Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted; the documented national pattern is raid-based arrest and public outing rather than individual stops. A High Court denied a request to declare the Sharia prohibition on cross-dressing unconstitutional, so the state layer remains legally contested rather than voided.

A constitutional challenge to the Sharia regime was pending as of late 2014 following the mass arrest of 16 trans women at a wedding on 8 June 2014.
tangentialFactors:
Kelantan's 2026 enactment belongs to a wider national pattern: all 13 states of Malaysia and the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya maintain Sharia enactments criminalising cross-dressing, passed since the 1980s, and three of them also bar women from posing as men. The Federal Court struck down Selangor's section 28 in February 2021 before striking down the 16 Kelantan provisions in February 2024, both on federalism grounds.

Enforcement against gender nonconformity is active and public across the country. In July 2020 the Religious Affairs Minister announced that the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department (Jawi) had his "full licence to carry out its enforcement actions" against transgender persons, an order the International Commission of Jurists demanded be revoked. In the Nur Sajat case, 122 religious officers were mobilised to pursue her for "insulting Islam" before she fled to Thailand and received UNHCR protection.

Queue-and-venue raids carry acute exposure risk. On 28 November 2025 police raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur, arresting 208 men under section 377B in the largest operation of its kind since 2022; media were pre-tipped, detainees' faces and personal details were leaked, and 17 civil servants identified among them were suspended. A magistrate rejected the remand extension as lacking ground, yet more than 130 people were held at one point including 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened. Justice For Sisters mobilised bailors and legal aid; on 2 December the Home Minister floated revisiting the provisions, and days later police raided another sauna in Penang.

Trans people in Malaysia face lethal violence and official indifference to it. A transgender woman was killed in Klang on 25 June 2019, the third killing of a trans woman in the country in fewer than two months; documentation of that case records police mistreatment and impunity under the heading "The Deceased Can't Speak for Herself".

The wider climate is one of state-backed restriction. Islamist opposition has foreclosed reform prospects, government-funded mukhayyam "rehabilitation" retreats had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021, and LGBT events and media content are censored. There is no same-sex marriage and no anti-discrimination law.
